reference_title: EM 1110-2-2104, Strength Design for Reinforced Concrete Hydraulic Structures (USACE, dated 1 November 2023, published 8 January 2025)

sections.title: Design assumptions and general requirements
sections.summary: General design procedure for members under combined loadings: loadings and reinforcement, eccentricity ratio, then the ϕPn and ϕMn equations of Appendix B for the member category (six categories: tension reinforcement only or both, in flexure and compression, tension and flexure, biaxial bending, flexure only). Eccentricity e′ = Mu/Pu + d − h/2 (Eq 4-1), measured from the tensile reinforcement, and ratio e′/d (Eq 4-2). εc = 0.003; ρ per paragraph 3-6; 0.85f′c over a = β1c; kb = β1 Es εc/(Es εc + fy) (Eq 4-3).
sections.body: [p. 29] a. This chapter covers general design requirements for the strength design of RCHS subject to combined loadings. The general design procedure for these members is: (1) Determine the member’s loadings and reinforcement configuration. (2) Determine the eccentricity ratio of the loading. (3) Design the member using the specified φPn and φMn equations for the given member and eccentricity ratio. b. Members subject to flexural and axial loads are considered in six categories: (1) Members that contain only tension reinforcement and are loaded in flexure and compression. Design of these members is covered in paragraph B-2. (2) Members with both tension and compression reinforcement and are loaded in flexure and compression. Design of these members is covered in paragraph B-3. (3) Members loaded in tension and flexure. Design of these members is covered in paragraph B-4. (4) Members that support axial loadings and are subject to biaxial bending. Design of these members is covered in paragraph 4-3. (5) Members that contain only tension reinforcement and are loaded in flexure only. Design of these members is covered in paragraph B-5. (6) Members that contain tension and compression reinforcement and are loaded in flexure only. Design of these members is covered in paragraph B-6. c. The eccentricity of axial load (e′) is a critical component in determining the effect that a given loading has on a member. (1) The eccentricity of axial load is a distance measured from the centroid of the tensile reinforcement, and is taken as: e′ = Mu/Pu + d − h/2 (4-1) where Pu is considered positive for compression and negative for tension. [p. 30] (2) For equation 4-1, the applied moment and axial loadings are the resultants of all applied loadings. Tension loadings and moments causing the bottom of the member to act in compression are taken as negative by convention. (3) The eccentricity ratio normalizes eccentricities such that a ratio of one represents an axial loading acting at the member’s extreme compression fiber, and a ratio of zero represents a loading acting directly at the centroid of tensile reinforcement. The eccentricity ratio for all members is defined as: e′/d (4-2) d. Additional general requirements that apply to all members covered by this chapter are: (1) The assumed maximum usable strain εc at the extreme concrete compression fiber must be equal to 0.003, according to ACI 318-19. (2) Balanced conditions for hydraulic structures exist at a cross section when the tension reinforcement ρb reaches the strain corresponding to its specified yield strength fy as the concrete in compression reaches its design strain εc. Tensile reinforcement must be provided such that ρ complies with paragraph 3-6. (3) Concrete stress of 0.85f′c must be assumed uniformly distributed over an equivalent compression zone bounded by edges of the cross section and a straight line located parallel to the neutral axis at a distance a = β1c from the fiber of maximum compressive strain, where c is the distance from the extreme compression fiber to the neutral axis. The free body diagrams shown in Figure B-1 through Figure B-3 illustrates these conditions. (4) Factor β1 will be taken as specified in ACI 318-19. (5) Factor kb represents the ratio of stress block depth (a) to the effective depth (d) at balanced strain conditions. Its value can be determined for all members using: kb = β1 Es εc/(Es εc + fy) (4-3) e. Appendix B contains the applicable design equations for each member type described in paragraphs 4-1a through 4-1d, along with the derivations of those equations.
key_points: The eccentricity of axial load is measured from the centroid of the tensile reinforcement: e′ = Mu/Pu + d − h/2 (Eq 4-1), Pu positive for compression and negative for tension (p. 29)
Eccentricity ratio e′/d (Eq 4-2): one represents an axial load at the extreme compression fiber, zero a load at the centroid of tensile reinforcement (p. 30)
The assumed maximum usable strain εc at the extreme concrete compression fiber must be equal to 0.003 (p. 30)
Tensile reinforcement must be provided such that ρ complies with paragraph 3-6 (p. 30)
kb, the ratio of stress block depth to effective depth at balanced strain: kb = β1 Es εc/(Es εc + fy) (Eq 4-3) (p. 30)

sections.title: Interaction diagrams
sections.summary: Introduces the P-M interaction diagram (compression failure, tension failure, and balanced point branches, Figure 4-1/4-2) and notes that diagrams can be built with the CGSI computer program or commercial software (demonstrated in Appendix C-4).
sections.body: [p. 30] a. An interaction diagram is a plot of the axial loads and bending moments that cause a concrete member of specified size and reinforcement to fail. Figure 4-1 diagrammatically shows the compression failure, tension failure, and balance point. [p. 31] Figure 4-2 shows strain condition at the compression failure, tension failure, and balance point. b. Interaction diagrams can be developed using the computer-aided software engineering program Concrete General Strength Investigation (CGSI) or commercial software. Appendix C includes an example using computer program CGSI. Figure 4-1. Interaction diagram with illustrated failure modes [p. 32] Figure 4-2. Interaction diagram illustrating strain conditions
key_points: An interaction diagram is a plot of the axial loads and bending moments that cause a concrete member of specified size and reinforcement to fail (p. 30)
Interaction diagrams can be developed using the program CGSI or commercial software (p. 31)

sections.title: Biaxial bending and axial load for all members
sections.summary: Biaxial bending with axial compression of square or rectangular sections: the Bresler load contour equation [Mnx/M0x]^K + [Mny/M0y]^K = 1.0 (Eq 4-4); for design, at Pn = Pu/ϕ, [Mux/(φM0x)]^K + [Muy/(φM0y)]^K ≤ 1.0 (Eq 4-5), with K = 1.5 for rectangular and 1.75 for square or circular members. M0x and M0y from paragraphs B-2 to B-4. Columns in biaxial bending should be circular where possible.
sections.body: [p. 32] a. Paragraph 4-3 applies to all reinforced concrete members subjected to biaxial bending. b. The load contour method and equation, known as the Bresler Approach, is used for investigation or design of a square or rectangular section that is subjected to an axial [p. 33] compression in combination with bending moments about both the x and y axes. The method is described in Bresler 1960. The Bresler load contour equation describing the capacity of a section with axial load and biaxial bending is: [Mnx/M0x]^K + [Mny/M0y]^K = 1.0 (4-4) where: Mnx, Mny = nominal biaxial moment strengths with respect to the x and y axes, respectively M0x, M0y = uniaxial nominal bending strength at Pn about the x and y axes, respectively For use in design, the equation is modified as shown in equation 4-5. For a given nominal axial load Pn = Pu/ϕ, the following nondimensional equation must be satisfied: [Mux/(φM0x)]^K + [Muy/(φM0y)]^K ≤ 1.0 (4-5) where: Mux, Muy = factored bending moments with respect to the x and y axes, respectively M0x, M0y = uniaxial nominal bending strength at Pn about the x and y axes, respectively M0x = capacity at Pn when Muy is zero; M0y = capacity at Pn when Mux is zero; K = 1.5 for rectangular members = 1.75 for square or circular members c. M0x and M0y are determined according to paragraphs B-2 through B-4 as applicable. d. Whenever possible, columns subjected to biaxial bending should be circular in cross section. If rectangular or square columns are necessary, the reinforcement should be uniformly spread around the perimeter. e. Appendix C includes an example of a rectangular column of axial load with biaxial bending using the computer program CGSI.
key_points: For a given nominal axial load Pn = Pu/ϕ: [Mux/(φM0x)]^K + [Muy/(φM0y)]^K ≤ 1.0 (Eq 4-5) (p. 33)
K = 1.5 for rectangular members; 1.75 for square or circular members (p. 33)
Whenever possible, columns subjected to biaxial bending should be circular; if rectangular or square, the reinforcement should be uniformly spread around the perimeter (p. 33)

sections.title: Mandatory requirements
sections.summary: Design of members for flexure and axial load must meet paragraph 4-1; design for biaxial bending and axial load must meet paragraph 4-3.
sections.body: [p. 34] a. Design of members for flexure and axial load must meet the requirements of paragraph 4-1. b. Design of members for biaxial bending and axial load must meet the requirements of paragraph 4-3.
key_points: Design of members for flexure and axial load must meet paragraph 4-1; for biaxial bending and axial load, paragraph 4-3 (p. 34)
